title: Projects
text:
Resilience-oriented Experimental–numerical Correlation Of Vibration, Energy, and Response
RECoVER is a research framework I am developing as part of my doctoral work in earthquake engineering. It connects field observations, ambient vibration measurements, structural modelling, and earthquake response simulations to investigate relationships between ground motion, structural response, and observed building damage.
My research focuses on low- to mid-rise reinforced-concrete school buildings, with a case study of the schools affected by the 2023 Türkiye earthquake sequence. Through RECoVER, I aim to bring experimental evidence and numerical analysis into a consistent workflow for studying earthquake damage.










Module
Full name
Role in the framework




SAVER
Seismic Ambient Vibration Evaluation for Resilience
Analyses ambient vibration measurements to identify structural vibration characteristics and provide experimental targets for model assessment.


DISASTER
Dynamic Inference and Simulation Analysis for Structural Transformation and Earthquake Response
Uses MATLAB and OpenSees to simulate structural response to earthquake ground motions and evaluate response demands, energy measures, and damage indices.


RESCuE
Response-backbone Extraction and Simulation Calibration Using ETABS
Processes ETABS pushover results to derive structural backbones and parameters for simplified nonlinear models.


SECURE
Structural Earthquake-sequence Calibration for Undamaged-state Reverse Estimation
Handshakes ETABS OAPI and MATLAB and also seeks to estimate undamaged structural properties by comparing simulated post-sequence vibration characteristics with field measurements.


PREPARE
Predictive Resilience and Earthquake Performance Assessment through Response Evidence
Explores machine-learning approaches for relating earthquake intensity and simulated structural response to observed damage.






Alongside the framework’s modules, I am developing PEnD, which stands for Period, Energy, Damping. It represents a proposed pair of measures: the intensity measure IM_PEnD and the damage index DI_PEnD.
This work investigates how period, energy, and damping can inform the characterization of earthquake demand and structural damage. The proposed measures are being developed and evaluated within RECoVER.



Developing this framework has strengthened my interest in reproducible computing, data analysis, and machine learning. My studies in computational linguistics are also motivating me to explore how information in technical documents could support future engineering research.
Project status: Active research and development. The modules are at different stages of implementation and validation. Project fuled by: Earthquake Engineering Research Facility

title: School buildings in my earthquake field research
text:
My PhD research examines relationships between earthquake ground motion, structural response, and observed building damage. As part of this work, RECoVER brings together field evidence and numerical analysis.
This post describes the building sample recorded in one snapshot of my field ambient-vibration review workbook. Before examining vibration characteristics, I want to understand which buildings and damage categories the dataset represents.

title: School buildings in my earthquake field research
text:
My PhD research examines relationships between earthquake ground motion, structural response, and observed building damage. As part of this work, RECoVER brings together field evidence and numerical analysis.
This post describes the building sample recorded in one snapshot of my field ambient-vibration review workbook. Before examining vibration characteristics, I want to understand which buildings and damage categories the dataset represents.

title: School buildings in my earthquake field research
text:
Data source and scope
The data come from the CASE_REVIEW sheet of my RECoVER_FieldAV_AdjudicationWorkbook_AR38D.xlsx research workbook.
The building-data CSV contains the selected columns used here. It retains the workbook’s building identifiers, reported storey counts, damage labels, and evidence routes.
This is a descriptive analysis of a research sample. It does not establish that building height caused a particular damage level. The workbook’s modal selections remain a separate review task.
This preliminary research sample is shared to demonstrate a reproducible analysis workflow for DSCI 521 Milestone 3 and my research portfolio. It represents a selected workbook snapshot, rather than the complete or final research dataset. The results describe this sample and should not be interpreted as final thesis findings.

title: School buildings in my earthquake field research
text:
Load the packages
I suppress package startup messages to keep the page readable. The analysis code and its results remain visible.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

title: School buildings in my earthquake field research
section: Read and inspect the building records
text:
Read and inspect the building records
Each row represents one building case. A station can be associated with more than one building, so I use CaseID to identify individual records.

buildings <- read_csv(
  "field-av-buildings.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

buildings |>
  select(CaseID, StoreysReported, FieldDamageLabel) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Building case", "Reported storeys", "Recorded damage")

Summarize the recorded damage categories
The table shows how many buildings fall in each recorded damage category, together with their mean and range of reported storey counts.

  summarise(
    buildings = n(),
    mean_storeys = mean(StoreysReported),
    minimum_storeys = min(StoreysReported),
    maximum_storeys = max(StoreysReported),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(

title: School buildings in my earthquake field research
text:
Compare the building sample visually
Point size represents the number of buildings sharing the same damage label and reported storey count.
Fractional storey counts are preserved as reported in the workbook. They have not been rounded or reinterpreted.

ggplot(
  buildings,
  aes(x = StoreysReported, y = FieldDamageLabel)
) +
  geom_count(colour = "#2563EB") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 9, breaks = c(1, 2)) +
  labs(
    x = "Reported number of storeys",
    y = "Recorded damage category",
    size = "Buildings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)







Figure 1: Reported storey counts by recorded damage category. Larger points indicate more buildings at the same position.

title: School buildings in my earthquake field research
text:
What does this snapshot show?
The sample includes buildings with several recorded damage levels. Moderate and low damage are the most common labels in this snapshot, while severe damage is represented by only one building.
The categories also overlap in reported storey count. These descriptive results do not isolate the effects of structural design, construction quality, or earthquake exposure.
For my research, this overview helps document the sample before moving to the separate tasks of reviewing vibration evidence and comparing structural models.

title: Do candidate vibration frequencies recur across recording windows?
text:
My PhD research uses ambient-vibration evidence to help characterize buildings affected by earthquakes. One useful review question is whether similar candidate frequencies appear in different portions of a recording.
Here, I examine frequency families assembled from early, middle, and late recording windows. A family groups nearby candidate frequencies within one building case. Recurrence can help prioritize further review, but it does not by itself confirm a structural mode.

title: Do candidate vibration frequencies recur across recording windows?
text:
Data source and scope
The data come from the FAMILIES sheet of my RECoVER_FieldAV_AdjudicationWorkbook_AR38D.xlsx research workbook.
The frequency-family CSV contains the selected fields used in this analysis, including building identifiers, frequency summaries, window counts, and review flags.
Each row represents one candidate frequency family, not one building. These are processed research records, rather than raw sensor measurements. The source workbook marks every family as not automatically accepted.
This preliminary research sample is shared to demonstrate a reproducible analysis workflow for DSCI 521 Milestone 3 and my research portfolio. It represents a selected workbook snapshot, rather than the complete or final research dataset. The results describe this sample and should not be interpreted as final thesis findings.

title: Do candidate vibration frequencies recur across recording windows?
text:
Load the packages
I use pandas for reading and summarizing the records and matplotlib for the figure.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import display

title: Do candidate vibration frequencies recur across recording windows?
text:
Read and check the records
I check the fields required for this analysis, verify that family identifiers are unique within each case, and confirm that window counts fall within the three recording windows.

families = pd.read_csv("field-av-frequency-families.csv")

required = [
    "CaseID",
    "FamilyID",
    "FrequencyMedian_Hz",
    "WindowsRepresented",
    "RelativeFrequencySpread_pct",
]

assert families[required].notna().all().all()
assert not families.duplicated(["CaseID", "FamilyID"]).any()
assert families["WindowsRepresented"].isin([1, 2, 3]).all()
assert families["FrequencyMedian_Hz"].gt(0).all()
assert families["RelativeFrequencySpread_pct"].ge(0).all()

overview = pd.DataFrame({
    "Frequency families": [len(families)],
    "Building cases": [families["CaseID"].nunique()],
    "Missing required values": [
        families[required].isna().sum().sum()
    ],
})

display(overview)

This snapshot contains 87 candidate frequency families across 13 building cases. Multiple families can belong to the same building.
The externally analysed case TK3144-12 is absent from this automatic family table. Its absence does not mean that the building has no vibration modes.

title: Do candidate vibration frequencies recur across recording windows?
text:
Count recurrence across windows
I count how many families appear in one, two, or all three windows. The percentage denominator is the total number of families.

recurrence = (
    families["WindowsRepresented"]
    .value_counts()
    .reindex([1, 2, 3], fill_value=0)
    .rename_axis("Windows represented")
    .reset_index(name="Frequency families")
)

recurrence["Percentage of families"] = (
    100 * recurrence["Frequency families"] / len(families)
).round(1)

display(recurrence)

There are 42 families represented in one window, 26 in two windows, and 19 in all three. Therefore, 45 of the 87 families appear in at least two windows.
These are family-level counts. Buildings contributing more families have more influence on this summary.

title: Do candidate vibration frequencies recur across recording windows?
text:
Visualize recurrence
The figure shows the number of families in each recurrence category. Integer labels above the bars make the counts explicit.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))

bars = ax.bar(
    recurrence["Windows represented"],
    recurrence["Frequency families"],
    color="#2563EB",
)

ax.bar_label(bars, padding=3)
ax.set(
    xticks=[1, 2, 3],
    xlabel="Number of recording windows represented",
    ylabel="Number of candidate frequency families",
    ylim=(0, 50),
)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Candidate frequency families represented in one, two, or three recording windows. Counts refer to families, not buildings.

title: Do candidate vibration frequencies recur across recording windows?
section: Examine frequency spread among recurring families
text:
Examine frequency spread among recurring families
Recurrence and frequency spread describe different aspects of the evidence. A family can recur across windows while its candidate frequencies vary.
For this comparison, I retain families represented in at least two windows. A family containing only one candidate necessarily has zero observed spread, which would not demonstrate repeatability.
I summarize the workbook’s recorded relative frequency spread. The values are percentages, not confidence intervals.

repeated = families.loc[
    families["WindowsRepresented"] >= 2
]

spread_summary = (
    repeated.groupby("WindowsRepresented")[
        "RelativeFrequencySpread_pct"
    ]
    .agg(["count", "median", "min", "max"])
    .rename(columns={
        "count": "Families",
        "median": "Median spread (%)",
        "min": "Minimum spread (%)",
        "max": "Maximum spread (%)",
    })
    .rename_axis("Windows represented")
    .reset_index()
    .round(2)
)

display(spread_summary)

The median recorded spread is approximately 1.77% for families represented in two windows and 3.39% for families represented in three windows.
This comparison involves different sets of families. It does not show that adding a window causes a larger spread. The grouping rule and number of candidate observations also affect the summaries.

title: Do candidate vibration frequencies recur across recording windows?
section: What does this mean for my research?
text:
What does this mean for my research?
In this snapshot, just over half of the candidate frequency families appear in more than one recording window. These recurring families provide a useful starting point for closer review.
However, the windows come from the same building recordings and are not independent building observations. Recurrence alone cannot identify a frequency as a translational or torsional structural mode.
For my RECoVER workflow, this analysis documents the available candidate evidence before reviewing directions, mode shapes, and other diagnostics. Final modal selections remain a separate task.

title: My first weeks
text:
My first weeks at UBC involved getting familiar with a broad set of tools. I have been working with Python, R, JupyterLab, Git, GitHub, and the Bash terminal. Although I have used computational tools in engineering research, learning how these tools fit together into a consistent workflow has brought new challenges.
One practical lesson has been that writing code is only part of the work. Running a notebook from beginning to end, rendering a document, and keeping track of changes all require attention. Setting up this website has helped me connect several of these steps: editing source files, previewing the result, and recording changes with Git.
As the program continues, I hope to become more confident with these workflows and spend more time exploring the questions they can help answer. I am especially interested in connections between NLP, earthquake engineering, earthquake seismology, and seismic hazards. For now, this website gives me a place to document what I am learning and reflect on my progress.
